13.2 Solutions to Exercises 2 - Exercises on groups Solution. (Question 2.5.1) Can prove by induction (which is long), or notice that: (g−1hg) n = (g−1hg)(g−1hg)(g−1hg)⋯(g−1hg)(g−1hg) = g−1h(gg−1)h(gg−1)h(gg−1)⋯h(gg−1)hg = g−1hng. Solution. (Question 2.5.2) (a) (⇒) By the Quick Subgroup Test, we know eG ∈ H. Therefore, if ∣H∣ = 1, then the unique element of H must be eG. (⇐) If H = ⟨eG⟩ then obviously ∣H∣ = 1. (b) Every element in H lies in G, we can write G = H ∪ S, where S ∩ H = ∅. Since G is finite and H ∩ S = ∅, we have ∣G∣ = ∣H∣ + ∣S∣. (⇒) If ∣G∣ = ∣H∣, then ∣S∣ = 0 and so S = ∅. Hence G = H. (⇐) If G = H then obviously ∣G∣ = ∣H∣. (c) No. For example, (Z, +) < (Q, +), but ∣Z∣ = ∣Q∣. Solution. (Question 2.5.3) We use the Quick Subgroup Test. [Identity] Since H and K are subgroups of G, we know (by the Quick Subgroup Test) that eG ∈ H and eG ∈ K. Hence eG ∈ H ∩ K. [Closure] If h, k ∈ H ∩ K, then h, k ∈ H and so hk ∈ H. Furthermore, h, k ∈ K and so hk ∈ K. Hence hk ∈ H ∩ K. [Inverse] Suppose h ∈ H ∩ K. Then h ∈ H so h−1 ∈ H. Furthermore, h ∈ K and so h−1 ∈ K. Hence h−1 ∈ H ∩ K for all h ∈ H ∩ K. Solution. (Question 2.5.4) Let n ∶= o(g). Now {g0, . . . , gn−1} = {g1, . . . , gn} ⊆ ⟨g⟩, so n ≤ ∣⟨g⟩∣. On the other hand, a general element of ⟨g⟩ has the form gm for some m ∈ Z. We can write m = an + r for some a ∈ Z and some 0 ≤ r < n by the division algorithm. Hence, gm = gan+r = (gn) a ∗ gr = e a G ∗ gr = gr ∈ {g0, . . . , gn−1}. Hence ∣⟨g⟩∣ ≤ n. The result is thus proved. Solution. (Question 2.5.5) (a) To answer this just calculate g0, g1, g2, . . . until you get a repeat — then you know you’ve found every element of ⟨g⟩. ⟨g⟩ = {e, (1 3 5 7)(2 4), (1 5)(3 7), (1 7 5 3)(2 4)} (b) To answer this just calculate (g2) 0, (g2)1, (g2) 2, . . . until you get a repeat — then you know you’ve found every element of ⟨g2⟩. ⟨g2⟩ = {e, (1 5)(3 7)} Solution. (Question 2.5.6) To prove it is cyclic, we need to find a single element that generates the group. Choose any element in Zn. It will have the form [m]n for some m ∈ {0, 1, . . . , n − 1}. Now because ⊕ is the group operation we have ([1]n) m = [1]n ⊕ ⋯ ⊕ [1]n (m times) = [1 + ⋯ + 1]n = [m]n. We have shown that every element in Zn lies in ⟨[1]n⟩. Hence Zn ⊆ ⟨[1]n⟩. On the other hand, we know ⟨[1]n⟩ ≤ Zn. Therefore Zn = ⟨[1]n⟩ and Zn is thus cyclic.
